$comment: AZURE FRONT DOOR (Premium) + WAF - the sole public edge.
Front Door is not optional (ADR-002, spec 2657). It is the only public DNS name and the only
public IP this platform has; APIM and both backends are private. A request that did not come
through here did not come from a client.
Placeholders in ${...} are substituted by the deployment pipeline. Nothing here is a secret.
The Front Door id below is an identifier, not a credential - it is checked at APIM to make the
origin specific to this platform, and its value being known to an attacker buys nothing while
the network control also holds. That is what 'neither control is sufficient alone' means in
practice (spec 10.3): each one is weak in a different direction.
Premium rather than Standard for one reason that matters here: Private Link to the APIM origin.
Standard cannot reach a private origin, which would force APIM to hold a public endpoint and
would reduce the first hop's network control to an IP-range filter.

profile.name: synthia-edge
profile.$comment: frontDoorId is emitted by the deployment and bound into the APIM named value `front-door-id`. The two MUST be the same value; build/scripts/check-edge-path.sh asserts the APIM policy reads that named value rather than a literal.

endpoints.name: synthia-customer-portal
$comment: THE CUSTOMER SURFACE GETS ITS OWN ORIGIN, and so does the staff surface (ADR-0009).
A browser's security boundary is the origin. Sharing one between the two portals would
share localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, service-worker scope and any script injected
into either - so a defect on the customer surface would reach a staff session's tokens.
Separate host names cost two more edge entries and buy the isolation the browser already
knows how to enforce.

endpoints.name: synthia-staff-portal
endpoints.$comment: The staff surface. See the customer endpoint for why these are separate origins.

originGroups.name: apim
$comment: THE ONLY ORIGIN THAT SERVES AN API, and it is APIM. There is no second route to a
backend, no 'internal' endpoint and no bypass for health. A backend origin added here
would be a path around the trust boundary that looks, in the portal, like a routing entry.
The two portal groups below serve static files and nothing else: no application data
reaches a browser except through this group, and build/scripts/check-edge-path.sh enforces
both halves - the origin allow-list, and that no portal route matches an /api path.

healthProbe.$comment: APIM's own built-in status endpoint. It reports the gateway, not an application, so it neither traverses nor bypasses the identity boundary.

sharedPrivateLinkResource.requestMessage: Front Door to APIM, the only origin path.
sharedPrivateLinkResource.$comment: Private Link, so APIM has no public ingress at all. This is the network half of the frontdoor-to-apim hop in build/policy/edge-trust.json; the X-Azure-FDID check in build/infra/apim/global.inbound.xml is the application half.

originGroups.name: customer-portal
$comment: THE CUSTOMER PORTAL BUNDLE. Static files: HTML, hashed JavaScript, hashed CSS, fonts.
It holds no data and reaches no database. Everything the surface displays it fetches from
the API host, through APIM, with the identity contract derived there as for any other
client - so this origin is not a second way into the platform, it is the delivery of the
code that calls the first one.
Private Link to a container app with INTERNAL ingress, exactly like APIM: the portal
container has no public FQDN of its own, so Front Door and its WAF cannot be stepped past.
The container serves the Stage 3 CSP baseline itself, with a per-response nonce, because
that policy cannot be expressed as a static edge header (ADR-0009, T346).

healthProbe.$comment: The portal host's own liveness endpoint - process-only, carries no identity contract and discloses nothing. The same path the Container App probes (build/docker/containerapps/customer-portal.yaml).

sharedPrivateLinkResource.requestMessage: Front Door to the customer portal container app.
sharedPrivateLinkResource.$comment: Private Link to the Container Apps environment. Without it the portal container would need public ingress, which build/docker/containerapps/*.yaml forbids and check-edge-path.sh rejects.

originGroups.name: staff-portal
originGroups.$comment: The staff portal bundle. Same shape and same reasoning as the customer group above; separate because the browser origin is the isolation boundary between the two surfaces.

sharedPrivateLinkResource.requestMessage: Front Door to the staff portal container app.

routes.name: api
$comment: ONE PATTERN, and it is the audience prefix set. /api/customer/v1, /api/staff/v1 and
/api/workload/v1 all match; nothing else does. A wildcard /* here would publish whatever
APIM happens to expose today and whatever it is given tomorrow.
Caching is deliberately absent. Every response on these paths is tenant-scoped, and a
shared edge cache keyed on URL is a cross-tenant leak waiting for two callers to request
the same path (constitution Principle: tenant isolation at every layer).

routes.name: customer-portal
$comment: A WILDCARD HERE, AND NOT ON THE API ENDPOINT. The difference is what sits behind each one:
this origin serves a directory of static files, and a single-page application must answer
every deep link with its index document. The API endpoint publishes the audience prefixes
and nothing else, because a wildcard there would publish whatever APIM is given tomorrow.
The portal endpoints carry no /api route at all - check-edge-path.sh asserts it. Were one
added, a client could reach the platform on a host where APIM never saw the request, which
is the bypass the single gateway exists to prevent.
CACHING IS DISABLED, and the reason is the nonce. Every document response carries a fresh
per-response CSP nonce, matched by the ngCspNonce attribute in the HTML; a cached document
would serve one user's nonce to everybody, which turns a per-response secret into a shared
constant and breaks style-src for every request the cache did not mint. The hashed asset
files are immutable and are cached by the browser on their own Cache-Control headers.

routes.name: staff-portal
routes.$comment: The staff bundle. Same reasoning as the customer route above, on its own origin.

securityPolicies.name: waf
$comment: ONE WAF POLICY, EVERY ENDPOINT. The portals are listed here for the same reason the API
is: a public host with no WAF in front of it is the one an attacker picks.
One policy rather than one per endpoint, deliberately. Two policies drift - a rule set
upgraded on the API and forgotten on the portals is a difference nobody sees until it is
read back months later, and the portal hosts would then be the weaker of the two.

policySettings.$comment: Prevention, not Detection. Detection mode is a WAF that writes reports about the attack it allowed through.

customRules.name: RateLimitPerClient
customRules.$comment: A ceiling, not the authorization control. APIM rate-limits again per caller, and neither is a substitute for the other: this one bounds an anonymous flood before it costs gateway capacity.

customRules.name: BlockSelfAssertedIdentityHeaders
$comment: DEFENCE IN DEPTH, AND NOTHING MORE. APIM deletes every inbound copy of the contract
unconditionally, so this rule is not what makes spoofing fail - it is what makes an
ATTEMPT visible at the outermost layer, in the WAF log, before it has consumed anything
further in.
It matches one header rather than all five on purpose. A caller forging identity sends
the tenant; matching the whole set here would duplicate, in a place nobody reviews
alongside the policy, a list whose single authoritative copy is edge-trust.json.
This rule MUST NOT be relied on as the anti-spoofing control. If APIM's deletion were
ever removed, a request with only X-Idp-Roles would pass here and reach a backend.
